title: CMA Tips and a Flip with Craig - July 22, 2026
summary: Live CMA training session where Craig walks through a flip property analysis in St. George, Utah. Covers CMA creation workflow, comp selection strategy, adjustment factors for ADUs and roofs, qualitative vs quantitative analysis, and detailed walkthrough of every adjustment category (bedrooms, bathrooms, square footage, basement, year built, garage, lot size). Also includes best practices for comp bracketing, handling data errors, and determining after-repair value for investment properties.

broker_guidance.guidance: Start by verifying MLS data against tax records. Copy the MLS number, create new CMA, populate form, and verify square footage, year built, lot size, and bedroom/bathroom counts before pulling comps.
broker_guidance.client_language: Let me verify the property details against tax records to make sure we're working with accurate data.

broker_guidance.guidance: Location is #1 priority. Then land size, then GLA (gross living area). Use polygon tool to carve out appropriate geographic boundaries. Exclude neighborhoods that are architecturally or demographically different. For older homes, expand year-built range (e.g., 1960-1990 for a 1977 home).
broker_guidance.client_language: I've selected comps from the immediate neighborhood with similar lot sizes and architectural styles.

broker_guidance.guidance: Always spot-check comp details. Agents sometimes enter garage counts as zero when they converted to ADU, or miss square footage entirely. Click into photos to confirm basement vs above-grade. Edit comp mode to fix errors before running adjustments.
broker_guidance.client_language: I noticed this comp shows zero garage spaces, but photos confirm a two-car garage. I've corrected that in the analysis.

broker_guidance.scenario: Valuing an ADU in a CMA
broker_guidance.guidance: A well-functioning ADU with outside entrance and off-street parking typically adds 5% of home value. Without outside entrance or shared laundry, reduce to 3-4% (e.g., $20-25K on a $500K home instead of $25-30K). In markets where basement ADUs are rare due to soil conditions, value may be higher.
broker_guidance.client_language: This property has a basement ADU. I'm valuing it at approximately $25,000, which is slightly conservative since it lacks a separate entrance.

broker_guidance.guidance: For flips, focus on the best-of-the-best comps (top 8 out of 30 if available). Don't waste time adjusting for current condition—just look at what fully remodeled homes sold for. If few comps exist, do full qualitative adjustments for kitchen, roof, flooring, and upgrades. Create custom adjustment factors for unique features.
broker_guidance.client_language: Based on the top remodeled comps in the neighborhood, your after-repair value should land around $550,000, with potential to push to $575K depending on finish quality.

broker_guidance.guidance: Bedroom differences are often picked up in square footage. A 4-bedroom vs 5-bedroom at identical square footage may actually favor the 4-bedroom if it means a larger family room. In condos/townhomes, bedroom count matters more—3-bed vs 2-bed can show distinct price differences. Default $1,000 per bedroom is a token adjustment.
broker_guidance.client_language: The bedroom count difference is minimal here because the square footage captures the value. In townhomes, I'd weight it more heavily.

broker_guidance.guidance: Buyers don't care much about 3/4 vs full bath difference. The master bathroom quality matters more—capture that in upgrades, not bathroom count. Half baths valued at ~$3,500. If a home has only one shower vs two, that could be a $15-20K deal killer regardless of bathroom count.
broker_guidance.client_language: The bathroom count is similar, but the master bathroom quality difference is significant—that's where I'll make the upgrade adjustment.

broker_guidance.guidance: Above-grade GLA at $75/sq ft is a baseline from appraisers. In luxury neighborhoods, go to $125-150+/sq ft. Basement square footage gets $30 for the space + $35 if finished = $65 total. Above-grade values more because of better light, higher ceilings, and perceived quality.
broker_guidance.client_language: I'm using $75 per square foot for above-grade living space, which is standard for this price range. Basements get $65 per finished square foot.

broker_guidance.guidance: $500/year is appropriate for newer homes (2023 vs 2022). For older homes (1970s-1980s), reduce to $100/year or even $0—buyers care about updates, not year. The difference between 1940 and 1950 is irrelevant; what matters is whether systems have been updated.
broker_guidance.client_language: For homes of this age, the year built adjustment is minimal. What matters more is whether the kitchen, roof, and systems have been updated.

broker_guidance.guidance: Garage bays used to be $5,000 each. Now in newer neighborhoods, $20-30K per bay is common when including lot premiums. In older neighborhoods, $10-15K per bay may work. Carports at ~$3,000 but adjust for size and quality. Always verify garage count in photos—agents sometimes misreport converted garages.
broker_guidance.client_language: I'm valuing the garage at $15,000 per bay based on this neighborhood's typical values.

broker_guidance.guidance: Default is $2/sq ft for land, but Craig prefers $3-4/sq ft. Small differences (0.24 vs 0.25 acre) are nominal. What matters more is lot quality—backing open space, views, usability. Location within neighborhood often trumps raw lot size.
broker_guidance.client_language: The lot sizes are similar enough that the raw square footage difference is nominal. What matters more is the location and usability of the lot.

broker_guidance.guidance: Watch for dysfunctional floor plans, 7-foot ceilings in 8-foot neighborhoods, busy roads, oversized power lines, super steep driveways, and excessive stairs. These don't show in standard CMA adjustments but can be massive deal killers. Create custom qualitative adjustments for these factors.
broker_guidance.client_language: I'm noting the steep driveway as a functional issue that could affect value. In this neighborhood, that's an unusual feature that buyers may discount.

steps: Verify MLS data against tax records before pulling comps
Use polygon tool to carve appropriate geographic boundaries for comp selection
Expand year-built range for older homes (e.g., 1960-1990 for 1977 home)
Delete bedroom/bathroom/garage filters initially to cast wider net
Spot-check comp data in photos—fix garage counts and square footage errors
Create custom adjustment factors for unique features (ADU, roof condition)
For flip analysis, focus on best-of-best remodeled comps
Set bedroom adjustments low ($1K) since value is captured in square footage
Capture bathroom quality differences in upgrades, not bathroom count
Use $75/sq ft for above-grade GLA, $65/sq ft for finished basement
Reduce year-built adjustments to $0-100 for older homes
Value garage at $15-20K/bay in older neighborhoods, $20-30K in newer
Use $3-4/sq ft for lot size differences rather than default $2
Watch for functional obsolescence and create custom qualitative adjustments
Save adjustment templates for future CMAs

objections.objection: There aren't enough comps in the immediate neighborhood
objections.response: Expand the geographic boundary carefully using the polygon tool, but exclude architecturally different areas. For older homes, you can go back 12 months. If still insufficient, look at total square footage rather than just GLA and consider whether the property is truly comparable.

objections.objection: The comp has a basement but others don't (or vice versa)
objections.response: Basement square footage gets $65/sq ft total ($30 for space + $35 if finished). Above-grade GLA values more because of better light and quality. If the subject is the only one with a basement, you'll need more comps or accept that appraisers may discount basement value.

objections.objection: How do I value an ADU without a separate entrance?
objections.response: Full ADU with outside entrance and parking = 5% of home value. Without separate entrance or with shared laundry, reduce to 3-4%. In markets where basement ADUs are rare, you might go higher. Always adjust based on functionality.

objections.objection: The seller thinks their home is worth more because it's newer
objections.response: For homes built in the 1970s-1980s, year built is almost irrelevant. What matters is updates. A 1977 home with a new kitchen and roof beats a 1985 home with original everything. Reduce year-built adjustments to $0-100 for older homes.

objections.objection: My CMA shows no adjusted values—what did I do wrong?
objections.response: You need to manually input adjustment values or load a saved template. The default CMA screen shows blank adjusted values. Create and save a template with your standard adjustments (bedrooms, bathrooms, sq ft, basement, year built, garage, lot size) so they auto-populate.
